rationale: The complete meeting abstract reports retrospective near-infrared prefrontal measurements during verbal fluency in patients with bipolar, depressive or schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. Oxygenated hemoglobin traces are the measured outcome. The abstract contains no Parkinson cohort or fig exposure.

The complete supplement separates abstract 000132, which detects hallucinations in ICU notes, from the FICUS family-support trial and a different perioperative diagnostic report. The 7,525-person ICU cohort is not a dried fig comparison. The primary article and the hallucination abstract report the same cohort.

The postmortem comparison classifies Lewy body disease, Alzheimer disease and controls and contrasts regional transcriptional alterations. Tissue gene-expression profiles provide no ingestive exposure or Parkinson visual episode-rate comparison.

The observational NACC data include 39 cognitive, behavioral and clinical measures across longitudinal profiles of Alzheimer and frontotemporal disorders. The study analyzes trajectories in phenotypic space without a dried fig intervention or food-timed Parkinson hallucination outcome.

UK Biobank analyses and genetic approaches compare hearing loss with subsequent Parkinson diagnosis risk, including hearing aid use as a separate observational variable. Auditory function and Parkinson incidence are distinct from Parkinson visual episode frequency after a food exposure.

A series of seven patients in six families describes clinical and imaging features of C19orf12-associated mitochondrial membrane protein neurodegeneration. Inherited parkinsonism and psychiatric features are observed in a different disease context without dietary fig comparisons.

The review compares PET tracer development for alpha-synuclein and imaging by synucleinopathy subtype. Its evidence concerns diagnostic signals and research limitations, without an ingredient exposure or clinical visual episode-frequency endpoint.

The review discusses published observations of viral infection and neurodegenerative disease, including possible associations and limitations. It contains no primary dietary fig intake comparison with Parkinson visual episode counts.

German outpatient claims identify 1,686,759 adults with incident dementia and 3,373,518 matched controls. Coded presentations over the preceding years measure diagnoses and signs, without specifying eaten figs or post-meal visual episode frequency.

The original compares Parkinson participants and controls on motor-network hierarchy and relates imaging features to spatial gene-expression data. The original endpoints are functional organization and motor findings, with no dietary intervention.

The reported early probable REM sleep behavior disorder group had a higher prevalence and greater later severity of hallucinations on clinical assessment. The report compares phenotype and severity over disease-time intervals. It does not count visual-only episodes after a food exposure.

The original review discusses incorporating biological markers into definitions of neuronal and glial synuclein disorders. The comparisons concern pathology, biomarker status and disease nomenclature. No dried fig exposure or visual episode frequency is measured.

The MDSGene review collates reported GBA1 variants and genotype–phenotype relationships in Parkinson, parkinsonism and Gaucher disease. Genetic classification and clinical reports provide no food intervention or timed visual episode outcome.

The bibliometric study analyzes publications and citation trends on Parkinson disease with depression. It counts literature records and research topics, with no clinical food exposure or visual episode comparison.

The original labels hallucination presence or absence from antemortem clinical notes and examines methylation networks in postmortem Parkinson brain tissue. It relates biology to recorded symptom occurrence without dried fig exposure or counts of recurrent visual episodes.

A longitudinal analysis follows 198 people with Parkinson and subjective cognitive complaints, selected from 326 without objective cognitive impairment. Its outcome is cognitive progression, with no dated dried fig intake or visual episode estimates after eating.

The extended follow-up of 202 people initially presenting with pure autonomic failure tracks sustained autonomic phenotype and conversion to other diagnoses. Timelines of autonomic and motor or cognitive features provide no culinary exposure comparison.

The review relates Alzheimer neuropathology, including coincident pathologies, to fluid and imaging biomarkers. Autopsy and diagnostic measures give no tested dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode rate.

ELEGANCE interim safety analysis covers 167 treated Parkinson patients. The narrative counts seven patients with any hallucination report and notes resolution in six. The adverse-event table separately codes visual hallucination and its serious subset. These are drug-treatment reports, not episode rates following dried fig.

Transcriptomic maps and network methods compare molecular targets of Parkinson and antipsychotic drugs grouped by clinical effects. The analysis projects drug targets and pathways rather than measuring food exposure or hallucination episodes in a clinical study.

A retrospective analysis of 22 people with dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy compares juvenile and adult onset and tracks motor milestones. Differences in psychiatric features belong to a different inherited disorder, with no dried fig exposure.

The Parkinson comparison group contributes MDS-UPDRS psychosis scores. The Cambridge Behavioural Inventory in other diagnostic groups separately asks about visual and auditory hallucinations and beliefs. Scale and group differences provide no food-attributed visual episode comparison.

Among 929 mixed Lewy body and Parkinson cognitive syndrome patients, the crude odds ratio linking microbleeds with visual hallucination presence was 1.264 with a confidence interval crossing one. The fully adjusted OR was 1.597 with 95% CI 1.014–2.517. This is diagnostic-cohort symptom presence, with no dietary exposure or recurrence measure.
The review describes how experimental brain organoids could model diverse synucleinopathy features. Cell and model observations supply no participant-level dried fig intake or clinical episode rate.

The MRI and biomarker comparison includes 57 participants in a Lewy body dementia spectrum clinical group and examines cortical microstructure and co-pathologies. Imaging abnormalities are separate from dietary fig exposure and clinical visual episode frequency.

A genetic and plasma biomarker study includes 151 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies and 2,010 controls. Genetic and blood markers are the comparative exposures. The paper supplies no individual fig intake or clinical episode change.

The study compares MRI measures of cholinergic white-matter hyperintensity with global white matter and other biomarkers along the Lewy body spectrum. Core clinical features are examined in relation to imaging, without a dried fig exposure or episode rate.

The study compares pathological alpha-synuclein detection in cerebrospinal fluid, skin, nasal material and urine across diagnostic groups. Assay sensitivity and specificity measure diagnostic performance, with no diet or hallucination exposure–outcome comparison.

The Parkinson and Lewy body comparison measures cerebrospinal fluid SERPIN E1 and examines associations with age and clinical features. Molecular concentration is different from measured food intake or visual recurrence after exposure.

Three of 958 patients in a psychiatry-based dementia cohort had pathological NOTCH2NLC expansions. Their case histories and diagnostic work-up describe different disorders and do not measure a response to dried fig consumption.

Antemortem MRI and autopsy of 54 participants compare substantia nigra susceptibility in 13 with Lewy pathology and 41 without. Imaging-based tissue iron estimates do not measure dietary iron, figs or a rate of visual episodes.

The literature review distinguishes sleep-transition hallucinations and psychiatric comorbidities in narcolepsy cohorts. It describes a separate sleep disorder and does not measure Parkinson visual episode frequency after fig consumption.

This review surveys investigational gene-based approaches in different dementias. The discussed interventions and biological targets are distinct from a dried fig exposure and reported Parkinson visual events.

A review compares alpha-synuclein seed amplification across specimens and diagnostic stages in Lewy body disease. The clinical focus is assay performance rather than an ingredient-specific visual outcome.

This review discusses barrier dysfunction in epilepsy and related experimental and clinical observations. Seizure and barrier measures do not establish a clinical Parkinson hallucinatory response following food.

The complete meeting publication includes separate cases of recurrent Charles Bonnet phenomena, severe malnutrition after sleeve gastrectomy, medication-associated perceptual symptoms and vision loss in a person with Parkinson. The original members do not connect measured dried fig intake to Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The review describes resting quantitative EEG signatures used to help distinguish prodromal or manifest dementia with Lewy bodies. It reviews diagnostic spectral patterns, not a culinary exposure or visual episode response over time.

The original study records intracranial EEG and elicited visual sensations in 69 people with medically refractory epilepsy selected for reporting an induced percept. The experimental comparison is stimulation-related physiology. It does not measure clinical Parkinson visual episodes or food exposure.

A clinical case with an identified VPS13C variant and a systematic review describe inherited Parkinson and parkinsonism phenotypes. The original comparison is genotype and case presentation, without dried fig intake or food-related visual outcomes.

The Canadian study assesses the Mild Behavioral Impairment Checklist in Parkinson and compares model structures and agreement with other clinical ratings. Visual and auditory items are separable. The authors report instability in the psychosis domain, and the design does not test any food.

A Parkinson group is compared while ON and OFF dopamine medication using functional gradients derived from brain imaging. The measured responses involve resting network organization under medication, with no dried fig exposure or visual episode-frequency endpoint.

The global review brings together published data on progressive supranuclear palsy prevalence, diagnosis, clinical features and care. Gaze abnormalities and disease progression in PSP do not supply Parkinson visual event rates after eating.

The TRANSEURO baseline imaging analysis maps neurotransmitter-related signals and network measures in 30 Parkinson participants. The study compares molecular imaging and resting functional connectivity without a food intervention or visual outcomes after eating.

The cross-sectional study compares 102 people with Parkinson and 88 matched controls on basal-ganglia functional gradients and clinical measures. Network reorganization and diagnosis status are distinct from an ingested ingredient and an episode-frequency outcome.

The review describes medication in endogenous Cushing syndrome, including management of excess cortisol and adverse effects. Its disease population and pharmacological interventions give no Parkinson outcome after eating figs.
The review considers positivity for synuclein assays in diagnoses beyond classic synucleinopathies. Its aim is interpreting disease markers, with no contemporary exposure-timed culinary comparison.

The original uses within-person levodopa or stimulation comparisons for reading speed and color contrast acuity. Immediate comparisons were generally inconclusive, with exploratory changes in selected conditions after surgery. The visual tasks do not count spontaneous hallucinations after eating.

In 165 Parkinson participants and 82 controls from PPMI, the study relates MRI thalamic subregion volumes to motor and cognitive performance. No individual dried fig exposure or visual recurrence comparison is reported. PPMI is shared with other imaging studies.

A prospective corticobasal syndrome cohort is classified by biomarker patterns and related clinical observations. The study identifies possible underlying pathologies and contains no dried fig intervention or clinical Parkinson visual episode outcome.

The review summarizes cholinergic basal forebrain anatomy and evidence from neurodegenerative disease sampling and pathology. Neuroanatomic descriptions and postmortem observations supply no effect estimate after dried fig intake.

This chapter reviews dopamine transporter ligands under investigation for psychostimulant use disorders. Its pharmacological targets, models and reported outcomes differ from a dried fig exposure and Parkinson visual symptoms.

The review examines septin proteins in neural development, cytoskeletal organization and neurological disorders. Molecular and cellular roles provide no measured dried fig ingestion or food-timed visual outcome.

Sequencing data from 15,684 individuals are screened for dystonia-related variants, with 45 carriers identified among the Parkinson group. Genetic risk assessment supplies no dietary exposure or episode-frequency comparison.

The Movement Disorder Society scoping review surveys outcome assessment instruments across 19 Parkinson constructs and 504 included studies. It discusses measurement and validation context, with no primary exposure or food-attributed episode-frequency measurement.

The analysis uses genetic instruments to examine medication use and different cognitive diagnoses. Its exposures are medication proxies and its endpoints are cognitive disorders, without any tested fig intake or visual symptom rate.

The sentence-comprehension fMRI study compares 25 people with mild cognitive impairment in Lewy body disease and 25 healthy controls. Language and processing measurements do not establish episode frequency or dietary exposure.

The original genotypes 3,058 Malaysian Parkinson participants, with detailed phenotyping in 185. The reported nonmotor comparison shows no group differences for visual hallucinations. This is a genetic subgroup comparison, with no tested dried fig consumption or timed clinical episode rates.

The narrative review synthesizes published differences in diagnosis, symptom profiles, progression and treatment in Lewy body disorders. Reported visual symptom differences are secondary clinical context without ingredient intake or measured food-timed recurrence.

The clinical imaging study examines resting hippocampal asymmetry and memory or smell in Parkinson participants with medication fluctuations. Cognitive and olfactory endpoints do not measure visual hallucination frequency or specify dried fig exposure.

The animal study assesses retinal and brain pathology after an experimental Parkinson-model exposure. Retinal pathology is measured directly, but the model cannot supply clinical participant reports of visual episodes with or without dried figs.

A family series describes five siblings with a new APP variant and case-level dementia phenotypes. The genotype and clinical trajectories concern inherited Alzheimer disease and contain no dietary fig exposure.

The machine-learning framework uses anatomical imaging features to model continuous diagnostic stages across Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia groups. Its performance measures are classification and staging, with no dietary or clinical visual-event contrast.

The review synthesizes differences in dementia with Lewy bodies clinical presentation, biomarkers and neuropathology. It distinguishes co-pathologies but contains no new dated food-intake or visual-episode comparison.
